title: How many hours of training does a California security guard need?
description: California BSIS guard card training: 8 hours of Power to Arrest and Use of Force before registration, 32 hours within six months, and 8 hours every year.
shortAnswer: A California security guard registered with the Bureau of Security and Investigative Services (BSIS) needs 8 hours of Power to Arrest and Appropriate Use of Force training before the registration is issued, 32 hours of security officer skills training within the first six months, and 8 hours of continuing training every year, at least 2 of which must review use of force. The requirements come from Business and Professions Code sections 7583.6 and 7583.7 and Title 16 CCR section 643.
keyTakeaways: The pre-registration course is 8 hours: Power to Arrest (3 hours) and Appropriate Use of Force (5 hours), with several use of force topics required to be taught in person.
The course exam must be passed with a score of 100% to count as successful completion.
Within 30 days of the registration card being issued or employment starting, a guard completes 16 hours (two mandatory courses); the remaining 16 hours follow within six months.
Annual continuing training is 8 hours and must include at least 2 hours reviewing appropriate use of force topics.

Guards keep their certificates until the registration expires or is canceled; employers keep records for the length of employment; training providers keep certificates and exam answer sheets for at least two years.
jurisdiction: United States (California): Private Security Services Act, Business and Professions Code sections 7580 onward, and Title 16 California Code of Regulations section 643
regulator: Bureau of Security and Investigative Services (BSIS), California Department of Consumer Affairs
appliesTo: Security guards employed by licensed Private Patrol Operators or private security employers
Proprietary private security officers, who follow the same skills training course under 16 CCR 643
Private Patrol Operators and proprietary security employers that deliver or arrange training
BSIS certified training facilities and Bureau-approved course providers
Guards carrying batons, tear gas or firearms, who need separate permits and courses

sections.heading: Who needs a California guard card?

blocks.text: Anyone employed by a licensed Private Patrol Operator (PPO) or private security employer to protect people or property, or to prevent theft, needs a security guard registration, commonly called a guard card. The BSIS [security guard fact sheet](https://www.bsis.ca.gov/forms_pubs/guard_fact.shtml) ties the role to Business and Professions Code (BPC) section 7582.1 and sets three eligibility conditions: being at least 18 (BPC 7582.8), passing a California Department of Justice and FBI background check, and completing the Power to Arrest training.

BSIS sits within the California Department of Consumer Affairs. Its training syllabus applies to both security guards and proprietary private security officers, so an in-house security team that falls under the proprietary rules follows the same course content and hours as contract guards.

sections.heading: What training is required before a guard card is issued?

blocks.text: Before BSIS issues the registration, the applicant must complete 8 hours of training: Power to Arrest (3 hours) and Appropriate Use of Force (5 hours). The BSIS [training syllabus](https://www.bsis.ca.gov/industries/g_train.pdf) says the course uses the Department of Consumer Affairs Power to Arrest and Appropriate Use of Force Training Manual dated July 2023, and that the course topics are those listed in BPC section 7583.7.

The use of force half is substantive rather than a formality. Its topics include the objectively reasonable force standard, the duty to intercede, de-escalation, implicit and explicit bias and cultural competency, interacting with people with disabilities or behavioral health issues, mental health and stigma, and active shooter situations. Four topics are marked for in-person delivery: the use of objectively reasonable force, use of force review and analysis, de-escalation and interpersonal communication, and scenario training.

blocks.title: Primary text: BSIS training syllabus
blocks.text: "Individuals required to take the Power to Arrest and Appropriate Use of Force Training shall take and pass an examination as provided in the Manual with a score of 100% in order to have successfully completed said training."

The fact sheet notes one practical exception: a registrant who cannot give their employing licensee the certificate for the power to arrest training must complete it within six months of their employment date. Employers should treat that as a remediation route for paperwork gaps, not as a reason to deploy untrained staff.

sections.heading: What does the 32 hour skills training cover, and when is it due?

blocks.text: The 32 hours of security officer skills training must be finished within the first six months of registration, on a 16 plus 16 schedule. According to the syllabus, two mandatory courses are due within 30 days of the registration card being issued or employment starting, and the other two mandatory four hour courses within six months; the remaining hours come from elective courses.

blocks.text: Each elective has a maximum number of hours that can be credited, for example two hours for Access Control and eight hours for the BSIS certified firearms course. Employer orientation and post orders can count as electives, which lets a PPO build site-specific content into the six month requirement.

sections.heading: What annual training must California guards complete?

blocks.text: Guards must complete 8 hours of continuing training every year under BPC 7583.6 and 16 CCR 643. The syllabus specifies that the annual training must include a minimum of two hours of review of the appropriate use of force topics, and that mandatory and elective courses make up the remaining hours.

Annual training can be delivered by an independent training entity or by the employer, and the syllabus says employer-provided training should be supported by evaluation of the guards' skills. Four hour elective courses may be expanded to eight hours for annual training, except Appropriate Use of Force, and a four hour baton refresher every other year can also count.

sections.heading: What training records must guards, employers and providers keep?

blocks.text: Records are split across three parties. The fact sheet says registered guards keep their certificates of completion until the registration expires or is canceled, and employers keep records for the duration of the guard's employment. Title 16 CCR section 643, in the [BSIS regulations compilation](https://www.bsis.ca.gov/about_us/laws/bsis_regulations.pdf), adds duties for whoever delivers the training.

items: Each certificate must name the courses, hours, issuing entity, individual, instructor and date, and state that the courses comply with the Department of Consumer Affairs skills training course.
Certificates must be serially numbered for tracking, and the provider keeps them for at least two years.
Providers keep exam results on Bureau-approved answer sheets for at least two years or until a Bureau inspection is completed, whichever comes first.
A PPO or proprietary employer that trains in house may train only its own direct employees, and its trainers must be qualified in the power to arrest and use of force topics.

blocks.text: Registrations also have a renewal clock: BSIS asks for the renewal application at least 60 days before expiry, and a registration not renewed within 60 days after expiration is canceled under BPC 7583.20, which means applying again from scratch.

sections.heading: How should a Private Patrol Operator track guard training?

blocks.text: A PPO's tracking should key every deadline to two dates per guard: the registration issue date and the employment start date. The table below is an illustrative template, not a BSIS form.

blocks.text: For the general method, see [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) and [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records). California employers with guards on site should also read [California workplace violence prevention training](/regulations/california-workplace-violence-prevention-training), which applies to most California employers separately from BSIS rules.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps each BSIS topic, such as the duty to intercede or de-escalation, to an assessable outcome, so annual use of force review can be targeted at the outcomes a guard performed weakest on rather than repeated wholesale. Post orders and employer policies become versioned content tied to the elective hours they satisfy. See [compliance programs](/programs/compliance).

faqs.q: Can a California guard start work before finishing the 32 hours?
faqs.a: Yes. The 32 hours of skills training is due within six months of registration, with 16 hours due within 30 days of the card being issued or employment starting. The 8 hour Power to Arrest and Appropriate Use of Force course, however, must be completed before BSIS issues the registration.

faqs.q: Can a California guard work before the registration card arrives?
faqs.a: BSIS says a person approved by the Bureau may work while waiting for the card if they carry a printout of the approval from the Bureau's website and valid photo identification, under BPC 7583.17. Cards usually arrive by mail about three weeks after the registration is issued.

faqs.q: Who can deliver California guard training?
faqs.a: Training can be delivered by a Bureau-approved organization or school, a licensed firearms training facility, or a Private Patrol Operator or proprietary security employer for its own direct employees, provided its trainers are qualified in the power to arrest and use of force topics.

faqs.q: Does the annual 8 hours have to be new content each year?
faqs.a: No. The BSIS syllabus says annual training may repeat previous courses or add new ones on topics applicable to private security work. The fixed element is that at least two of the eight hours must review appropriate use of force topics.
